title: Inca khipu record-keeping
summary: Khipus were knotted, coloured cords used by the Inca Empire as a data-recording device. Officials used them for censuses, tribute and other accounts; trained khipu makers produced and read them, and runners carried them between way stations. Knot rows follow a base-10 system. Surviving Inca khipus date to about 1400-1534, and any narrative content remains undeciphered.

uncertainty.note: NIST gives 1400-1534 A.D. for surviving Inca khipus and 1450-1534 for the empire; Hyperallergic says the surviving khipus date from the 15th to 16th centuries. Start 1400 is the earlier bound; the id year 1450 is only a lookup key.

where.modern_name: Cusco, Peru (reference point; the empire ran from the Pasto region of Colombia to Santiago, Chile)
where.historical_name: Inca (Inka) Empire, Andes of South America

importance.justification: The Inca Empire ran its administration on a knotted-cord recording system, an important non-alphabetic record-keeping technology.

sources.title: Historic Measures: How Standards and Technology Enabled the Inca Empire to Thrive

sources.title: Unraveling the Lost Inca Language of Knots

reviewer_note: Least sure: the point is Cusco as a reference marker for an empire spanning thousands of km; no opened page names Cusco as a khipu site. NIST (1,000 khipus) and Hyperallergic (600 survive) differ on counts, so none is stated.
